t: Maximum Repeating Substring: Count Consecutive Word Blocks
o: word is k-repeating when word concatenated k times appears somewhere inside sequence, and we want the largest such k. Example 1: abab in ababc gives k = 2; example 2: ba occurs but baba does not, so k = 1; example 3: ac never occurs, so k = 0. Two facts shape the search space: a k-repeating block has length k * |word|, so k can never exceed floor(|sequence| / |word|), and any occurrence of the repeated block is anchored at some start index. With strings of at most 100 characters, checking every candidate k with a substring containment test is instant; the DP alternative instead asks, for each end position, how many consecutive word copies END there, which reuses overlapping information and scales if constraints grow.
k: The answer is capped at len(sequence) // len(word) — longer concatenations cannot fit.
k-repeating means one CONTIGUOUS run: ba is 1-repeating in ababc even though b and a alternate throughout.
DP over end positions: dp[i] = dp[i - |word|] + 1 when word ends at i, giving runs of consecutive blocks.

a.n: Approach 1: Try Every k from Largest to Smallest
a.i: Build word repeated k times for the largest feasible k and test whether sequence contains it; decrease k until something matches or k reaches 0. Each containment test is O(n * m) with naive search (fast built-in implementations in practice), and there are at most n/m tests. Simple to state, hard to get wrong, and returns immediately on success thanks to scanning from the top.
s: For k = limit down to 1, form rep = word * k.
If sequence contains rep as a substring, return k.
a.t: O((n / m) * n * m) worst case with naive matching — at most n/m containment checks over an O(n)-length text (n = |sequence|, m = |word|); effectively instant for n, m <= 100.
a.sp: O(n) — one repeated-block buffer no longer than sequence.

a.n: Approach 2: DP on Runs Ending at Each Index
a.i: Define dp[i] as the number of consecutive word-copies that end exactly at index i of sequence. If the substring ending at i spells word, then dp[i] extends whatever run ended m characters earlier: dp[i] = dp[i - m] + 1, else dp[i] = 0. The answer is the maximum over all positions. This does O(n) constant-work steps beyond the substring comparison and naturally reports partial overlaps like example 2 without any retry loop.
s: Let m = len(word); initialize dp array of size len(sequence) with zeros.
For each i from m-1 to len(sequence)-1, compare sequence[i-m+1 .. i] with word.
On match, dp[i] = (i >= m ? dp[i-m] : 0) + 1; otherwise dp[i] stays 0.
Track and return the maximum dp value seen.
a.t: O(n * m) — each of n end positions compares up to m characters against word.
a.sp: O(n) — the dp array over sequence indices.

w: For interview purposes either solution passes; quote Approach 1 in thirty seconds, then offer Approach 2 as the scalable version since it avoids rebuilding candidate strings and degrades gracefully. Pitfalls: confusing k-repeating with counting total occurrences scattered across sequence (runs must be contiguous and aligned); off-by-one at run boundaries where i - m goes negative; forgetting the empty case returns 0 rather than erroring. Edge cases: word longer than sequence answers 0; identical single-character strings answer n. Follow-up: raise lengths to 10^5+ and the intended tool becomes KMP or Z-function matching of word against sequence plus a run-length pass over match positions.
